availability.body: Instead of scanning the board, say when you are free: the whole event, the same hours every day, or a handful of dates. Pick one and the grid underneath changes to match, then press Save. Organisers read this while they build the schedule, so you stop being offered the mornings you were never going to make.
availability.title: Or let the shifts find you

bookIt.body: No form, no approval, no waiting to hear back. Press it and the block turns green on your board and the count goes up on everybody else's. Handing it back is the same single press, which is what stops anyone being left holding a name that cannot come. Press it now if you like — the tour carries on either way.
bookIt.title: Taking it is one press

finish.body: Jobs are cut into shifts, you take the ones that fit, and your availability fills the gaps you never went looking for. The buttons here take you straight back to the jobs and to your own shifts. The demo is yours until it expires, and nothing you do in it reaches anybody else.
finish.title: That is the whole model

jobRow.body: The left of this row is the job itself: what it is called, where it happens, how many places are still open. The rest of the row is the same job spread across the days of the festival, and each small block in it is one shift. Reading down the page shows you where people are still missing.
jobRow.title: One row, one job

jobsIntro.body: A job is something that has to be covered over a stretch of time: a welcome desk across a whole weekend, a café counter on the Saturday. Nobody signs up for a job as a whole. wirksam cuts each one into individual shifts, and a shift is what you take. This screen is both of those at once.
jobsIntro.title: Jobs, and the shifts under them

myBookings.body: Past and upcoming together, each with the time, the place and who else is on it, which is what you actually want on the morning of. This is also where you hand a shift back if something changes. Which leaves the other half of the deal: nobody should have to go hunting for the shifts that fit them.
myBookings.title: Everything you said yes to

nextShift.body: The demo has put you on a few shifts, and the nearest one sits at the top of every visit: the time, the place, and how many others will be there with you. It is the one thing most helpers open this page to check. Where those shifts come from is the next screen.
nextShift.title: What you are already down for

openChip.body: One block is one shift: the start time, and underneath it the places taken out of the places needed. This one still has room. The pale ones are already covered and the green ones are yours, which is how you read a whole weekend without opening anything. Press below and I will open this one.
openChip.title: A shift with room in it

shiftRoster.body: A shift is not an empty slot, it is a small group with room left in it. This list is the people who have said yes, and the blank line is what is still going spare — knowing you would be the third of four rather than the only one is usually what settles it. Where to go and anything to bring sit just above.
shiftRoster.title: Who is already on it

welcome.body: This is Riverside Summer Festival, a three-weekend village festival run entirely by volunteers, and you are one of them. Everything it needs doing is broken into jobs — the screen calls them tasks — and every job is cut into shifts you can take one at a time. Nothing here is real, and nothing you do reaches anybody else.
welcome.title: You are inside a real event

attention.body: Shifts nobody has taken yet, shifts still short of a pair of hands, and anyone waiting to be let into the event. Every line is a count that is also a link, so this is a to-do list rather than a status board — and when none of it applies, the panel is not there at all. Below it sits every open shift, soonest first.
attention.title: What needs you this week

finish.body: Describe a job once, let wirksam cut it into shifts, watch the thin ones, and read afterwards how it went. Nothing you have seen is a mock-up — the demo event behaves exactly as a real one would, and the person at the door is still waiting. It is yours until it expires, and no real event is touched by anything you do in it.
finish.title: That is the whole loop

formIntro.body: Creating a job is this single page, folded into five sections: what the job is, which event it belongs to, which days it runs, how each day is cut up, and a preview of the result. The first two are filled in already, this event included, so the rest has something to work with. Nothing is saved until you say so.
formIntro.title: One form, one job

generateShifts.body: The daily window, how long one shift should run, and how many people it needs. From those three, every shift on every day you picked is worked out, down to the odd half hour left at the end. Change the shift length here and watch the count in the preview move — this is the step that saves you typing forty rows by hand.
generateShifts.title: This is where shifts come from

jobRow.body: A job is something that has to be covered over a stretch of time: a welcome desk across a whole weekend, a café counter on the Saturday. You describe it once, on the left of this row. The rest of the row is wirksam's work — the same job cut into individual shifts, day by day.
jobRow.title: One row, one job

people.body: Each row is somebody who can see the schedule, and the role beside the name says what they may do with it: members take shifts, admins build the schedule too, and the owner can hand the whole event on. Above this is the person the dashboard mentioned, still waiting to be let in — accept, and they can start taking shifts straight away. The invitation card below is the one thing on this tour you can look at but not use: the demo sends no email at all.
people.title: The people in your event

reporting.body: How much of the schedule filled, the hours people gave, who took on the most, and which times of day were hardest to cover. Beside it is a spreadsheet export for anyone who would rather do their own arithmetic. Useful in the week afterwards, and more useful still when you plan next year's.
reporting.title: How it actually went

shiftPreview.body: Every shift your settings would produce, counted here and laid out below, before a single one exists. Tap one to leave it out — the Sunday morning nobody works. Fixing a two-hour block that should have been one costs nothing now, and a great deal once forty people have booked into it. Saving is the button at the bottom; the tour leaves that to you.
shiftPreview.title: Check before you commit

staffing.body: Each block carries the places taken over the places needed, so a whole weekend's staffing is one downward glance. This one is still short of people; the pale ones are done. That is your list for the week before, and it is the same board a volunteer is looking at. Next comes the form all of this came out of — it arrives folded into sections, and I will open them one at a time.
staffing.title: Reading the schedule at a glance

taskDates.body: A single day, a run of days, or a few dates scattered across the event — the last one is what a festival with gaps in it actually looks like. A short run has been picked for you, inside the event's own window, which is why the calendar will not offer you anything outside it. Everything you set after this happens on each of the days chosen here.
taskDates.next: How the day is cut up
taskDates.title: Which days it runs

welcome.body: Riverside Summer Festival, half staffed: four jobs, a schedule cut into shifts, and a handful of volunteers already on it. Your side of this is two habits — describing the work once, and then watching where it is still uncovered. The second one starts just below.
welcome.title: You are running this event
